## Problem

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be open and let

$$
f\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega).
$$

Define

$$
T_f(\varphi)
=
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx,
\qquad
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
$$

Prove that $T_f$ is a distribution on $\Omega$.

## Solution

Recall that a distribution on $\Omega$ is a continuous linear functional on

$$
\mathcal D(\Omega)
=
C_c^\infty(\Omega).
$$

We show that $T_f$ is well-defined, linear, and continuous.

### Well-definedness

Let

$$
\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).
$$

Since $\varphi$ has compact support, there exists a compact set

$$
K\subset\Omega
$$

such that

$$
\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset K.
$$

Because

$$
f\in L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega),
$$

we have

$$
\int_K|f(x)|\,dx<\infty.
$$

Moreover, $\varphi$ is bounded on $K$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_\Omega |f(x)\varphi(x)|\,dx
&=
\int_K |f(x)\varphi(x)|\,dx\\
&\leq
\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty(K)}
\int_K|f(x)|\,dx\\
&<\infty.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence $T_f(\varphi)$ is well-defined.

### Linearity

Let $\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_f(a\varphi+b\psi)
&=
\int_\Omega
f(x)\bigl(a\varphi(x)+b\psi(x)\bigr)\,dx\\
&=
aT_f(\varphi)+bT_f(\psi).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus $T_f$ is linear.

### Continuity

Let

$$
\varphi_j\to0
\quad\text{in }\mathcal D(\Omega).
$$

By the definition of convergence in $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, there exists a compact set

$$
K\subset\Omega
$$

such that

$$
\operatorname{supp}\varphi_j\subset K
$$

for all sufficiently large $j$, and

$$
\sup_{x\in K}
|D^\alpha\varphi_j(x)|
\to0
$$

for every multi-index $\alpha$.

In particular, taking $\alpha=0$,

$$
\|\varphi_j\|_{L^\infty(K)}
\to0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
|T_f(\varphi_j)|
&=
\left|
\int_K f(x)\varphi_j(x)\,dx
\right|\\
&\leq
\int_K|f(x)||\varphi_j(x)|\,dx\\
&\leq
\|f\|_{L^1(K)}
\|\varphi_j\|_{L^\infty(K)}\\
&\to0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus

$$
T_f(\varphi_j)\to0.
$$

Hence $T_f$ is continuous on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$.

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
T_f\in\mathcal D'(\Omega).
}
$$

Thus every locally integrable function defines a distribution.

## Remark

A distribution induced by a locally integrable function is called a **regular distribution**.

We usually identify $f$ with its associated distribution and simply write

$$
\langle f,\varphi\rangle
=
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.
$$

This identification is injective: if

$$
\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx=0
$$

for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then

$$
f=0
$$

almost everywhere in $\Omega$.

Thus

$$
L_{\mathrm{loc}}^1(\Omega)
\hookrightarrow
\mathcal D'(\Omega).
$$
